```{r linear-mixed-models-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
library(car)
library(DHARMa)
library(effectsize)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(emmeans)
library(performance)
library(patchwork)
library(janitor)
library(tidyverse)

options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))
options(scipen = 999)  # no sci notation

u_df <- read_csv("data/andrew.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  # Map to Quinn & Keough's Table 9.1 densities. NOTE the file's dens_33 /
  # dens_66 labels are the reverse of the book's percentages -- verified by
  # matching patch means: dens_33 is the book's 66% group, dens_66 its 33%.
  mutate(treat = case_when(
           treat == "removal" ~ "0%",     # book   0% density, mean algae 39.2
           treat == "dens_66" ~ "33%",    # book  33% density, mean algae 19.0
           treat == "dens_33" ~ "66%",    # book  66% density, mean algae 21.6
           treat == "control" ~ "100%"),  # book 100% density, mean algae  1.3
         treat = factor(treat, levels = c("0%", "33%", "66%", "100%")),
         patch = as_factor(patch))

u_summary <- u_df %>%
  group_by(treat) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(algae), sd = sd(algae),
            se = sd / sqrt(n), min = min(algae), max = max(algae))
```

And from the ANOVA weeks — **factorial designs**:

Today the second factor is **not** crossed with the first, and we do not

Last week changed the **distribution** of the response. This week

independent. Put both together and you get `glmer()`.
:::

Part 1 builds the **hierarchical** design, and the traditional

## Part 1 · The Data, and Why a One-Way ANOVA Fails It {.divider}

## Data Overview {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
`treat` — urchin density treatment (0 / 33 / 66 / 100%)
`patch` — **four patches nested inside each treatment, 16 in all**
`quad` — 5 replicate quadrats within every patch
`algae` — % cover of filamentous algae, the response

```{r linear-mixed-models-02}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
head(u_df, 4)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-03}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
u_summary %>%
  dplyr::select(treat, n, mean, sd) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

::: callout-note
**📖 The gradient is not monotonic**

39.2 → 19.0 → 21.6 → 1.3. The 33% and 66% means sit within noise of
each other. That is the data, not an error — and it is part of why the
treatment effect comes out non-significant.
:::
:::
:::::

## The Design Is Hierarchical, Not Factorial {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
`treat` and `patch` are **not crossed**. Patch 7 exists only inside one
treatment; there is no "patch 7 of the 0% treatment *and* of the 100%
treatment."

That is a **nested**, or hierarchical, design:

$$\text{treatment} \rightarrow \text{patch} \rightarrow \text{quadrat}$$

The 5 quadrats in a patch are **subsamples of that patch**, not 5
independent replicates of the treatment. The treatment was applied to
the **patch**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**⚠️ So what is *n*?**

For testing `treat` there are **16** experimental units, not 80. Four
patches per treatment.

Treating the 80 quadrats as independent replicates of the treatment is
**pseudoreplication** (Hurlbert 1984) — the single most common fatal
flaw in ecological statistics.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 The giveaway question**

*"What did I apply the treatment to?"* Count those. If you measured
more things than you manipulated, the extra measurements are
subsamples.
:::
:::
:::::

## Pseudoreplication, Priced {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Same 80 numbers, two models. The only difference is what the treatment
is tested against:

```{r lmm-pseudo-01}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
a_ps <- summary(aov(algae ~ treat + treat:patch,
                    data = u_df))[[1]]

round(a_ps[, c("Df", "Sum Sq", "Mean Sq")], 1)

c(naive_F  = a_ps[1, "Mean Sq"] / a_ps[3, "Mean Sq"],
  nested_F = a_ps[1, "Mean Sq"] / a_ps[2, "Mean Sq"]
  ) %>% round(2)
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**16.11 against 2.72**

Both divide $MS_{treat}$ = 4810. The **naive** model divides by
$MS_{resid}$ = 298.6, the quadrat-to-quadrat noise. The **correct** one
divides by $MS_{patch(treat)}$ = 1770.2, the patch-to-patch noise.

*p* goes from **0.00000007** to **0.091** — from a headline result to
nothing — on exactly the same data.
:::

The traditional fix is to name the error stratum by hand:

``` r
aov(algae ~ treat + Error(patch), data = u_df)
```

**That is what the rest of this lecture replaces.**
:::
:::::

## Where the Variation Goes

::::: columns
::: {.column width="42%"}
One quadrat's distance from the grand mean splits into **three** pieces,
not two:

$$\underbrace{(Y_{ijk} - \bar{Y})}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{(\bar{Y}_i - \bar{Y})}_{A} + \underbrace{(\bar{Y}_{ij} - \bar{Y}_i)}_{B(A)} + \underbrace{(Y_{ijk} - \bar{Y}_{ij})}_{\text{resid}}$$

Square and sum over all 80 quadrats:

$$SS_{total} = SS_A + SS_{B(A)} + SS_{resid}$$

On these data: **54 781 = 14 429 + 21 242 + 19 110**.

::: callout-note
**The middle row is the whole point**

A one-way ANOVA has no $SS_{B(A)}$ row — that variation lands in the
residual. Here it is **bigger than the treatment effect**, and it is
what the treatment must be tested against.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r lmm-pseudo-02}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-alt: "Four stacked panels showing the nested sums-of-squares allocation on the sea urchin data. Panel one, SS total: every quadrat's deviation from the dashed grand-mean line. Panel two, SS_A: each of the four treatment means' deviation from the grand mean. Panel three, SS_B(A): each of the sixteen patch means' deviation from its own treatment mean. Panel four, SS residual: every quadrat's deviation from its own patch mean."
ss_df <- u_df %>%
  arrange(treat, patch) %>%
  mutate(patch = fct_inorder(patch)) %>%
  group_by(treat) %>% mutate(treat_mean = mean(algae)) %>%
  group_by(treat, patch) %>% mutate(patch_mean = mean(algae)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(grand = mean(algae), x = as.numeric(patch))

pm <- ss_df %>% distinct(treat, patch, x, patch_mean, treat_mean, grand)

tm <- ss_df %>%
  group_by(treat) %>%
  summarise(x = mean(x), xmin = min(x) - 0.45, xmax = max(x) + 0.45,
            treat_mean = first(treat_mean), grand = first(grand),
            .groups = "drop")

set.seed(42)
pts <- ss_df %>% mutate(xj = x + runif(n(), -0.22, 0.22))

base <- function(p, ttl) {
  p +
    scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = tm$x, labels = levels(ss_df$treat)) +
    labs(title = ttl, x = NULL, y = "Algae (%)") +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-5, 82)) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 9, face = "bold"),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}

p1 <- base(
  ggplot(pts) +
    geom_segment(aes(xj, xend = xj, y = grand, yend = algae, colour = treat),
                 alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_point(aes(xj, algae, colour = treat), size = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = ss_df$grand[1], linetype = "dashed"),
  expression(SS[total] * ": every quadrat vs. grand mean"))

p2 <- base(
  ggplot(tm) +
    geom_segment(aes(x, xend = x, y = grand, yend = treat_mean, colour = treat),
                 linewidth = 1.1) +
    geom_segment(aes(xmin, xend = xmax, y = treat_mean, yend = treat_mean,
                     colour = treat), linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = ss_df$grand[1], linetype = "dashed"),
  expression(SS[A] * ": treatment means vs. grand mean"))

p3 <- base(
  ggplot(pm) +
    geom_segment(aes(x, xend = x, y = treat_mean, yend = patch_mean,
                     colour = treat), linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(aes(x, patch_mean, colour = treat), size = 1.4) +
    geom_segment(data = tm, aes(xmin, xend = xmax, y = treat_mean,
                                yend = treat_mean),
                 linewidth = 0.5, colour = "grey30"),
  expression(SS[B(A)] * ": patch means vs. their treatment mean"))

p4 <- base(
  ggplot(pts) +
    geom_segment(aes(xj, xend = xj, y = patch_mean, yend = algae,
                     colour = treat), alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_point(aes(xj, algae, colour = treat), size = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_segment(data = pm, aes(x = x - 0.35, xend = x + 0.35, y = patch_mean,
                                yend = patch_mean),
                 linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey30"),
  expression(SS[residual] * ": quadrats vs. their own patch mean"))

p1 / p2 / p3 / p4
```
:::
:::::

## Pseudoreplication Corrupts the *p*-Value, Not the Effect Size {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r lmm-pseudo-03}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
e_nested <- eta_squared(
  aov(algae ~ treat + Error(patch), data = u_df))$Eta2_partial
e_naive <- eta_squared(
  aov(algae ~ treat + patch, data = u_df))$Eta2_partial[1]

data.frame(
  model = c("Nested (correct)", "Naive (pseudoreplicated)"),
  partial_eta2 = round(c(e_nested, e_naive), 2),
  p = c("0.091", "0.00000007"))
```

The wrong model and the right model agree the treatment effect is
**large** — 0.40 against 0.43.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**What they disagree about is confidence**

Seven orders of magnitude in *p*, and almost nothing in effect size.
Pseudoreplication does not invent an effect. It invents **certainty**.
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 So what is the honest conclusion?**

Not "urchins do not affect algae." It is **"a large effect that four
patches per treatment could not resolve"** — a power problem, and the
effect size is what lets you say so.

Hold onto that. In Part 5 the variance components will tell you
*exactly why* four patches were not enough, and what to do about it.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 2 · Fixed, Random, and the Mixed Model {.divider}

## What Makes an Effect "Random"?

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
Ask one question: **do I care about these specific levels, or are they a
sample of levels I could have had?**

::: {.compact-table}
| | `treat` | `patch` |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| The levels are | 0/33/66/100% density | patches 1–16 |
| Chosen by | me, deliberately | whatever was there |
| Would a repeat study use the same ones? | **yes** | no — different patches |
| I want to estimate | **each level's mean** | **how much they vary** |
| So it is | **fixed** | **random** |
:::

::: callout-important
**The key consequence**

A fixed factor with 16 levels costs you **15 parameters**. A random
factor with 16 levels costs you **one** — a single variance,
σ²~patch~.

That is why mixed models cope with designs `aov()` chokes on: they are
estimating far less.
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 A useful test**

If you can write a sentence a reader would care about that names a
specific level — *"the 100% density treatment reduced algae"* — it is
**fixed**.

If the sentence would be *"patch 7 happened to be lush"* — nobody cares
about patch 7 in particular. **Random.**
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ You need enough levels**

Estimating a variance from **fewer than ~5 levels** is unreliable. With
2 or 3 groups, fit them as fixed effects instead.

We have 16 patches — comfortably enough.
:::
::::
:::::::

## Reading the Random-Effects Formula

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Read every random term as

$$(\ \text{what varies}\ \mid\ \text{across what}\ )$$

- **`(1|patch)`** — the `1` means the **intercept**. Each patch gets its
  own baseline algae cover.
- **`(1|treat:patch)`** — the same thing, just naming the group as the
  treatment-patch combination. Still intercept-only.
- **`(1 + depth|patch)`** — *this* is a random **slope**: each patch gets
  its own intercept **and** its own slope for `depth`. (There is no
  `depth` in this dataset — it is what one would look like.)
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ `(1|treat:patch)` is not a random slope**

Anything of the form `(1|...)` is **random intercepts only** — the `1`
*is* the intercept. What changes between `(1|patch)` and
`(1|treat:patch)` is the **grouping variable**, not what varies within
it.

Here they are the identical model, because patch IDs are already unique
(1–16) and each patch sits in one treatment. We will use `(1|patch)`.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 The rule**

You only have a random slope when something **other than `1`** appears
on the left of the `|`.
:::
:::
:::::

## Fitting It {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-05}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
u_lmer_model <- lmer(
  algae ~ treat + (1 | patch),
  data = u_df,
  control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

VarCorr(u_lmer_model)

fixef(u_lmer_model)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
The model in words:

$$algae_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + b_{j(i)} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$

- $\mu$ — the overall mean
- $\alpha_i$ — the **fixed** effect of treatment *i*
- $b_{j(i)}$ — the **random** effect of patch *j* in treatment *i*,
  $b \sim N(0,\ \sigma^2_{patch})$
- $\epsilon_{ijk}$ — the residual for quadrat *k*,
  $\epsilon \sim N(0,\ \sigma^2_{within})$

::: callout-important
Notice what the model estimates for `patch`: **not 16 numbers, one
number** — the variance those 16 patches were drawn from.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 3 · Testing the Fixed Effect {.divider}

## Two Tests, Two Answers {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-06}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
Anova(u_lmer_model, type = 3,
      test.statistic = "F")
```

```{r linear-mixed-models-07}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
Anova(u_lmer_model, type = 3,
      test.statistic = "Chisq")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**The *F*-test** (Kenward-Roger denominator df)

- Accounts for the uncertainty in the estimated variance components
- More conservative, better at small *n*
- Here: *F*~3,12~ = 2.72, ***p* = 0.091**

**The Wald χ²**

- Assumes the variance components are **known**, not estimated
- Assumes **infinite** denominator df, i.e. a large sample
- Here: χ²~3~ = 8.15, ***p* = 0.043**

χ² = *F* × numerator df = 2.717 × 3 = 8.15 — exactly. The only thing
that differs is the **reference distribution**: χ²~3~ assumes infinite
denominator df; *F*~3,12~ admits there are 12.
:::
:::::

## Same Model, Same Data, Opposite Conclusions

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.compact-table}
| Test | Statistic | *p* | Verdict at α = 0.05 |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| *F*, Kenward-Roger df | *F*~3,12~ = 2.72 | **0.091** | not significant |
| *F*, Satterthwaite df | *F*~3,12~ = 2.72 | **0.091** | not significant |
| Wald χ² | χ²~3~ = 8.15 | **0.043** | significant |
:::

**Rule of thumb: default to the *F*-test.** As the number of groups
grows its denominator df grow with them, and it converges on the χ² — so
you give up nothing by always using it, and you are protected when the
sample is small. The χ² is a **large-sample shortcut**, not a better
test.

We have **80 observations and 16 patches** — nowhere near large sample.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**⚠️ Report the *F*-test — and say which df you used**

The χ² is being over-confident. It pretends it knows σ²~patch~ and
σ²~within~ exactly, when they were estimated from 16 patches.

The *F*-test agrees with Part 1's `aov(Error(patch))` to four decimal
places, **because it is the same test**.
:::

::: callout-warning
**🖐 The uncomfortable part**

Run only the χ² and you report a significant effect and never know.
When two defensible analyses straddle α = 0.05, say so and justify the
choice — do not pick one and delete the other.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 4 · How the Variance Actually Gets Estimated {.divider}

## The Question This Part Answers

For three weeks, **every** answer came from one move: take the total
sum of squares, cut it into pieces by source, divide each piece by its
df to get a mean square, and form a ratio.

$$SS_{total} = SS_{treat} + SS_{patch(treat)} + SS_{within}$$

`lmer()` printed σ²~patch~ = 294.3 and never showed you a sum of
squares anywhere.

::: callout-important
**So where did that number come from, and why is it not an SS table?**

The rest of this part is the answer. It is the single biggest
conceptual change between Part 1 and the rest of today — bigger than
the notation, bigger than the *p*-value.
:::

## The Old Route — Sums of Squares and Expected Mean Squares {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Part 1's table, one more time:

```{r lmm-ems-01}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
a_tab <- summary(aov(algae ~ treat + treat:patch,
                     data = u_df))[[1]]
round(a_tab[, c("Df", "Sum Sq", "Mean Sq")], 1)
```

Statistical theory tells you what each mean square estimates **on
average** — its *expected* mean square:

$$E[MS_{within}] = \sigma^2_{within}$$
$$E[MS_{patch}] = \sigma^2_{within} + n\,\sigma^2_{patch}$$
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
Now **set the observed equal to the expected and solve.** That is all
the old method is — two equations, two unknowns, no statistics at all
past this point:

$$\hat\sigma^2_{within} = MS_{within}$$
$$\hat\sigma^2_{patch} = \frac{MS_{patch} - MS_{within}}{n}$$

```{r lmm-ems-02}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
MS_patch  <- a_tab[2, "Mean Sq"]
MS_within <- a_tab[3, "Mean Sq"]
n <- 5                      # quadrats per patch

c(within = MS_within,
  patch  = (MS_patch - MS_within) / n)
```

This is the **method of moments**. It is arithmetic on a table.
:::
:::::

## The New Route — Write Down the Variance and Search for It

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
A mixed model never builds that table. It writes the variance of the
**whole response vector** in one matrix:

$$\mathbf{V} = \sigma^2_{patch}\,\mathbf{ZZ}^\top + \sigma^2_{within}\,\mathbf{I}$$

- $\mathbf{Z}$ says which patch each quadrat belongs to
- $\mathbf{ZZ}^\top$ is 1 for any two quadrats **in the same patch**,
  0 otherwise
- So $\mathbf{V}$ states, directly, that two quadrats in a patch are
  correlated and two in different patches are not

Then it asks a completely different question:

> **Which pair of numbers (σ²~patch~, σ²~within~) makes the data I
> actually observed most likely?**
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**That is the whole switch.**

**Old:** partition a quantity you computed (SS), then solve an algebraic
identity for the variances.

**New:** propose a pair of variances, ask how probable the data are
under them, and keep searching until that probability stops improving.

No decomposition. No table. **A search over a likelihood surface.**
:::

The *F*-ratio idea does not disappear — it comes back at the end, when
you test the fixed effect. But it is no longer how the variances are
obtained.
:::
:::::

## The Restricted Likelihood, Written Out {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
Eight lines, no `lme4`. This is literally what the optimizer is doing:

```{r lmm-reml-01}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
y <- u_df$algae
X <- model.matrix(~ treat, u_df)   # fixed effects
Z <- model.matrix(~ 0 + patch, u_df)   # grouping
ZZt <- Z %*% t(Z)

reml_ll <- function(v_patch, v_within) {
  V  <- v_patch * ZZt + v_within * diag(nrow(X))
  Vi <- solve(V)
  A  <- t(X) %*% Vi %*% X
  b  <- solve(A, t(X) %*% Vi %*% y)     # GLS fixed effects
  r  <- y - X %*% b
  -0.5 * as.numeric(determinant(V, log = TRUE)$modulus +
                    determinant(A, log = TRUE)$modulus +
                    t(r) %*% Vi %*% r)
}
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
Three pieces, each doing one job:

- $\log|\mathbf{V}|$ — penalises making the variances big, since a
  bigger variance spreads probability thinner
- $\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}$ — penalises leaving big
  residuals, which pushes the variances **up**
- $\log|\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}|$ — the
  **restricted** part, the correction for having estimated the fixed
  effects

The answer is the pair where those forces balance.

(An additive constant, $-\tfrac12 (n-p)\log 2\pi$, is left out — it
shifts the curve but not where the maximum is.)
:::
:::::

## The Surface the Optimizer Climbs

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r lmm-reml-02}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-alt: "Curve of the restricted log-likelihood against sigma-squared patch, rising steeply from a low value at zero, peaking near 294, and then declining very gradually. A dashed vertical line marks the maximum."

prof <- tibble(v = seq(0, 1200, length.out = 180)) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(ll = reml_ll(v, 298.6)) %>%
  ungroup()

best <- prof$v[which.max(prof$ll)]

ggplot(prof, aes(v, ll)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 294.31, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  annotate("text", x = 294.31, y = min(prof$ll), hjust = -0.08,
           label = "REML peak\n294.3", size = 2.9, color = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = expression(sigma[patch]^2),
       y = "Restricted log-likelihood") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
Slice the surface at σ²~within~ = 298.6 and you can see the whole
method: the optimizer walks uphill until the slope is flat.

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Look how flat that peak is**

Everything from roughly 150 to 600 sits within about **one
log-likelihood unit** of the peak. **Variance components are badly
determined with only 16 groups** — and that uncertainty is exactly what
the Kenward-Roger *F*-test accounts for and the Wald χ² ignores.

This plot is the reason those two tests disagreed.
:::
:::
:::::

## Both Routes, One Number {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-reml-03}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
# route 1: moments, from the SS table
moments <- (MS_patch - MS_within) / n

# route 2: maximise the restricted likelihood
fit <- optim(c(200, 300),
             \(p) -reml_ll(p[1], p[2]),
             method = "L-BFGS-B",
             lower = c(0, 1e-6))

# route 3: what lmer() reports
lmer_vc <- as.data.frame(
  VarCorr(u_lmer_model))$vcov[1]

round(c(moments = moments,
        likelihood = fit$par[1],
        lmer = lmer_vc), 3)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**294.31, three ways.**

They agree to within **0.001** — and the first two have **nothing in
common** methodologically. One is algebra on a table of sums of
squares; the other is a numerical search over a likelihood surface.

On a **balanced** design the restricted maximum-likelihood solution has
a closed form, and that closed form *is* the moment estimator — as long
as it comes out positive.
:::

So the traditional route was never wrong. It was a special case that
happens to have a shortcut — and you have been using the shortcut without being told it
was one.

**Next slide: what happens when the shortcut stops existing.**
:::
:::::

## Where the Two Routes Part Company {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
**1. The moment estimator can return a negative variance.**

$MS_{patch} < MS_{within}$ is perfectly possible by chance, and then
$(MS_{patch}-MS_{within})/n$ is **below zero** — an impossible value for
a variance.

```{r lmm-reml-04}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
set.seed(11)
fake <- expand_grid(treat = factor(1:4), p_in = 1:4, quad = 1:5) %>%
  mutate(patch = factor(paste0(treat, "_", p_in)),
         y = rnorm(n(), 10, 5))          # patches truly identical

ft <- summary(aov(y ~ treat + treat:patch, fake))[[1]]
fm <- lmer(y ~ treat + (1 | patch), fake,
           control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

round(c(moments = (ft[2, "Mean Sq"] - ft[3, "Mean Sq"]) / 5,
        REML    = as.data.frame(VarCorr(fm))$vcov[1]), 3)
```

REML cannot go below zero — the likelihood is only defined for
non-negative variances — so it stops at the boundary and warns
**"boundary (singular) fit"**.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**2. Unbalanced data has no single *n* to divide by.**

Thin four patches to one quadrat each, as a storm would:

```{r lmm-reml-05}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
thin <- u_df %>% filter(!(patch %in% c(2, 6, 10, 14) & quad > 1))
tt <- summary(aov(algae ~ treat + treat:patch, thin))[[1]]
tm <- lmer(algae ~ treat + (1 | patch), thin,
           control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

MSp <- tt[2, "Mean Sq"]; MSw <- tt[3, "Mean Sq"]
round(c(`moments, n = 5`    = (MSp - MSw) / 5,
        `moments, n0 = 3.95` = (MSp - MSw) / 3.95,
        REML                 = as.data.frame(VarCorr(tm))$vcov[1]), 1)
```

::: callout-important
Three answers, and the moment estimator needs you to **choose** an
effective *n* before it will give one at all. REML never asks — the
likelihood already knows how many quadrats each patch has.

**This is why mixed models replaced `Error()`.**
:::
:::
:::::

## Why REML and Not Plain ML {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-reml-06}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
ml_fit <- lmer(algae ~ treat + (1 | patch),
               data = u_df, REML = FALSE,
               control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

round(c(
  REML = as.data.frame(VarCorr(u_lmer_model))$vcov[1],
  ML   = as.data.frame(VarCorr(ml_fit))$vcov[1]), 1)
```

Plain maximum likelihood estimates σ²~patch~ as **205.8**. REML gets
**294.3**. ML is biased **30% low**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
You have met this bias before, in week 2.

$$s^2 = \frac{\sum(y-\bar y)^2}{n-\mathbf{1}} \quad\text{not}\quad \frac{\sum(y-\bar y)^2}{n}$$

Dividing by *n* under-estimates the variance because you spent one df
estimating $\bar y$. **ML makes exactly that mistake**, at scale: it
estimates the four treatment means and then behaves as though they were
known all along.

::: callout-important
**REML = "restricted"**: it maximises the likelihood of the data
*after* the fixed effects have been projected out — the
$\log|\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}|$ term three slides back.
That term **is** the $n-1$ correction, generalised.
:::

**Use REML for variance components. Switch to ML only to compare models
with different fixed effects.**
:::
:::::

## Part 4 — The Short Version

::: {.compact-table}
| | **Nested ANOVA (Part 1)** | **Mixed model (Parts 2–7)** |
|------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| Starts from | the total sum of squares | the variance matrix $\mathbf{V}$ |
| Core move | **partition** SS by source | **search** for the most likely variances |
| Variance components from | solving $E[MS]$ equations | maximising the restricted likelihood |
| Needs balance? | **yes**, for exact tests | no |
| Negative variance | can happen, is meaningless | impossible — stops at 0 |
| Unbalanced *n* | you must pick an effective *n* | handled automatically |
| On this dataset | σ²~patch~ = 294.31 | σ²~patch~ = 294.31 |
:::

::: callout-note
**✅ The one sentence**

Sums of squares *divide up* variation that has already been computed;
likelihood *proposes* variances and asks how well they explain the data.
On a balanced design the two land on the same number — everywhere else,
only the second one still works.
:::

## Part 5 · What the Random Effect Buys You {.divider}

## The Intraclass Correlation {.tight-code}

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-04b}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(u_lmer_model))
v_patch <- vc$vcov[vc$grp != "Residual"]
v_resid <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Residual"]

round(c(among_patches  = v_patch,
        within_patches = v_resid,
        ICC = v_patch / (v_patch + v_resid)), 3)
```

The **ICC** is the share of variance living *between* groups —
equivalently, **how strongly two quadrats in the same patch resemble
each other**.
::::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**ICC = 0.50 is the whole reason we are here**

Two quadrats from the same patch are **half-correlated**. They are not
two independent observations.

An ICC near 0 would mean patches barely matter and ordinary ANOVA would
have been fine. An ICC of 0.50 means ignoring patch would have been
badly wrong — and Part 1's naive model showed exactly how wrong
(*F* = 16.11 instead of 2.72).
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Use it to design the next study**

With ICC = 0.50, a sixth quadrat in an existing patch buys you almost
nothing. A **new patch** buys you a lot. The *p*-value could never have
told you that.
:::
::::
:::::::

## Partial Pooling — What Happens to Each Patch

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
A random effect does not just adjust the *p*-value. It changes each
patch's **estimate**.

```{r linear-mixed-models-04c}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.2
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: "Slope plot comparing each patch's raw observed mean algae cover to its shrunken mixed-model estimate, with lines joining the two; estimates move toward their treatment mean, and patches with more extreme raw means move furthest."
raw_means <- u_df %>%
  group_by(treat, patch) %>%
  summarise(raw = mean(algae), .groups = "drop")

raw_means$fitted <- predict(u_lmer_model,
                            newdata = raw_means[, c("treat", "patch")])

raw_means %>%
  pivot_longer(c(raw, fitted), names_to = "kind", values_to = "algae") %>%
  mutate(kind = factor(kind, c("raw", "fitted"),
                       c("raw patch mean", "model estimate"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(kind, algae, group = patch, color = treat)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Algae cover (%)", color = "Treatment") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 New word: shrinkage**

Every patch estimate is pulled **toward its treatment mean**. The model
treats an extreme patch average as partly real signal and partly luck,
and splits the difference.

Patches with fewer quadrats, or more internal scatter, get pulled
further.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Why this is a feature**

A patch whose 5 quadrats happened to land high is probably *not* that
extreme — the next 5 would come back closer to average.

This is **partial pooling**: between treating every patch as unrelated
and pretending they are all identical.
:::
::::
:::::::

## Reporting the Variance Components

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: callout-note
**How to report this result**

"Algal cover did not differ significantly among urchin density
treatments (linear mixed model with patch as a random effect,
***F*~3,12~ = 2.72, *p* = 0.091**, Kenward-Roger denominator df).
Among-patch variance was substantial (**σ²~patch~ = 294.3** vs
**σ²~within~ = 298.6**, ICC = 0.50), indicating strong spatial
heterogeneity in algal cover."
:::

Both halves belong in the sentence. The fixed effect answers *did the
treatment do anything*; the variance component answers *how noisy is
this reef*, which is what the next person planning a study needs.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**⚠️ "Not significant" is not "no effect"**

With σ²~patch~ ≈ σ²~within~, patch-to-patch variation is as large as
quadrat-to-quadrat variation. Four patches per treatment simply cannot
resolve a treatment effect against that much background noise.

The honest conclusion is **"this design could not detect it"**, not
"urchins do not affect algae."
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Where 294.3 came from**

By hand from the mean squares, from a restricted likelihood maximised
with `optim()`, and from `VarCorr()` — three routes, one number.
See Part 4.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 6 · Post-Hoc, Assumptions, and Reporting {.divider}

## Estimated Marginal Means {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-09}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
u_emm <- emmeans(u_lmer_model, ~ treat)
u_emm
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
Every standard error is **9.41** — identical across treatments, because
the design is balanced and the SE comes from the **patch** stratum
(4 patches per treatment), not from the 20 quadrats.

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Two of these intervals go below zero**

Algae cover is a percentage. It cannot be negative.

The mixed model fixed the **error structure** and left the
**distribution** alone — it still assumes normal, unbounded response.
Last week you fixed the distribution and left the error structure alone.
Real data often needs both: that is `glmer()`.
:::
:::
:::::

## Post-Hoc Comparisons {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-11}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
multcomp::cld(u_emm, alpha = 0.05, Letters = letters)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**Every treatment shares the letter `a`.**

No pair is distinguishable. That is the correct and expected result —
the omnibus *F*-test was already non-significant (*p* = 0.091), so there
was nothing for a post-hoc to find.

Running post-hocs after a non-significant omnibus test is **exploratory
only**. Report it as such, or not at all.
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 Read the pattern, not a ranking**

The means run 39.2 → 19.0 → 21.6 → 1.3. The two middle treatments are
effectively tied, so this is **not** a clean monotonic gradient. Resist
the temptation to write one.
:::
:::
:::::

## Diagnostics 1 — `check_model()` First {.tight-code}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-12}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.0
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-alt: "The performance package's check_model output for the urchin mixed model, with three panels: a normal Q-Q plot of the residuals whose tails bend away from the line, a Q-Q plot of the sixteen patch random effects which sit close to their line, and a homogeneity-of-variance panel whose trend rises from left to right."
check_model(u_lmer_model,
            check = c("qq", "reqq", "homogeneity"))
```
:::

::::: {.column width="44%"}
The same one call as every other model this term — and on a `merMod` it
adds a panel you have not seen before.

::: callout-note
**📖 The `reqq` panel is the new one**

A mixed model assumes **two** things are normal: the residuals *and the
random effects*. `reqq` is a Q-Q plot of the 16 patch intercepts, and it
is the only diagnostic here that looks at them.

```{r lmm-diag-01}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
check_normality(u_lmer_model,
                effects = "random")
```

Reassuring — but it is 16 numbers. Report it, and say that 16 levels
cannot carry a strong claim either way.
:::
:::::
::::::

## Diagnostics 2 — Why Those Residual Tests Mislead {.tight-code}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-diag-02}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
check_normality(u_lmer_model)

check_heteroscedasticity(u_lmer_model)
```

Both scream *p* < .001. **Neither number means what it would mean for an
`lm()`.**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**⚠️ The reference distribution is wrong**

Those tests ask: *are these residuals iid normal with constant
variance?* For an `lm()` that **is** the assumption. For a mixed model
it is **not**:

- Conditional residuals are **shrunk** toward zero by partial pooling,
  so they are not even supposed to have variance σ²~within~
- How much each one shrinks depends on its patch's *n* and the ICC
- So a non-normal, non-constant-variance pattern is partly **what the
  model does on purpose**

Shapiro and Breusch–Pagan have no way to know that. They compare your
residuals against a yardstick that does not apply.
:::
:::
::::::

## Diagnostics 3 — DHARMa Builds the Right Yardstick {.tight-code}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Instead of assuming a reference distribution, **simulate** it from the
fitted model:

```{r lmm-diag-03}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.0
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-alt: "DHARMa diagnostic output for the urchin mixed model: a Q-Q plot of scaled residuals against a uniform reference with the KS, dispersion and outlier test results printed on it, beside a plot of scaled residuals against predicted values with quantile regression lines."
set.seed(42)
sim <- simulateResiduals(u_lmer_model, n = 1000)
plot(sim)
```

1. Simulate 1000 new datasets from the fitted model
2. For each observation, ask **what quantile of its own simulated
   distribution** the real value sits at
3. Under a correct model those quantiles are **Uniform(0, 1)** — always
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**✅ Why this is better**

The yardstick is **generated by your model**, so it already contains the
shrinkage, the unequal group sizes, the ICC — everything that broke the
tests on the last slide.

And "should be uniform" holds for **any** model: `lmer`, `glmer`,
Poisson, negative binomial, zero-inflated. You learn **one** diagnostic
instead of one per family.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Keep `check_model()` anyway**

It is faster to read, and `reqq` is genuinely useful. Use it to **look**,
and DHARMa to **decide**.
:::
:::
::::::

## Diagnostics 4 — What DHARMa Actually Concluded {.tight-code}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r lmm-diag-04}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
testUniformity(sim, plot = FALSE)$p.value

testDispersion(sim, plot = FALSE)$p.value

testOutliers(sim, plot = FALSE)$p.value
```

```{r lmm-diag-05}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
# test at the level of the experimental unit
sim_patch <- recalculateResiduals(
  sim, group = u_df$patch)

testUniformity(sim_patch, plot = FALSE)$p.value
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.compact-table}
| Test | *p* | Verdict |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Shapiro, residuals | **< 0.001** | wrong yardstick |
| Breusch–Pagan | **< 0.001** | wrong yardstick |
| DHARMa uniformity | **0.022** | mild deviation |
| DHARMa dispersion | **0.64** | fine |
| DHARMa outliers | **1.00** | none |
| DHARMa, by patch | **0.092** | fine |
:::

::: callout-important
**The honest summary changed**

Not "this model fails two assumptions at *p* < 0.001". It is **"a mild
distributional deviation, no dispersion problem, no outliers, and
nothing wrong at the level of the 16 patches."**

Same model, same data. The second description is the defensible one.
:::

**`recalculateResiduals(group =)`** is the mixed-model-specific move:
the treatment was applied to **patches**, so test there too.
:::
::::::

## Heterogeneity of Variance {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-13}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
leveneTest(algae ~ treat, data = u_df)
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ This test ignores `patch`**

`leveneTest()` has no idea the quadrats are grouped. It is testing the
80 raw values as if they were independent — the very assumption this
whole lecture exists to fix. Read it as a **description** of the raw
spread, not as a test of the mixed model.

The model's own diagnostic is the residuals-vs-fitted plot, and DHARMa.
:::

Variances really are unequal (the 100% treatment has SD 3.2, the 0%
treatment 28.7). Quinn & Keough noted the same thing, tried
transformations including arcsine, and found none that fixed it — so
they analysed the untransformed data and said so. A balanced ANOVA is
reasonably robust to this. **Say it out loud in the methods rather than
hoping nobody checks.**
:::
:::::

## Visualization

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-14}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| fig-width: 4.0
#| fig-height: 3.1
#| fig-alt: "Boxplot of algae cover by urchin density treatment with jittered quadrat points overlaid, showing high cover and wide spread in the 0% treatment and near-zero cover in the 100% treatment."
ggplot(u_df, aes(x = treat, y = algae, fill = treat)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.85) +
  labs(x = "Urchin density treatment", y = "Algae cover (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-15}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| fig-width: 4.0
#| fig-height: 3.1
#| fig-alt: "Model estimated marginal means with 95% confidence intervals by treatment, with the sixteen individual patch means plotted behind them, showing the patch means scatter widely within every treatment."
ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = raw_means, aes(treat, raw),
              width = 0.12, alpha = 0.55, size = 2, color = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(data = as.data.frame(u_emm),
                  aes(treat, emmean, ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL),
                  color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8, size = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = "Urchin density treatment", y = "Algae cover (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```

**Grey** — the 16 patch means. **Red** — the model's treatment means and
95% intervals. The grey scatter *within* each treatment is σ²~patch~;
it is why the red intervals are so wide.
:::
:::::

## Part 7 · Wrap-Up {.divider}

## The `lmer` Formula Cheat-Sheet

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
Read every random term as **`( what varies | across what )`**.

::: {.compact-table}
| Formula | Meaning |
|------------------|------------------------------------|
| `y ~ x + (1|g)` | random **intercept** per group |
| `y ~ x + (1 + x|g)` | random intercept **and slope** |
| `y ~ x + (0 + x|g)` | random slope only, shared intercept |
| `y ~ x + (1|a) + (1|b)` | two **crossed** random factors |
| `y ~ x + (1|a/b)` | b **nested** in a — shorthand for `(1|a) + (1|a:b)` |
:::

Random **slopes** and time-series error structures get their own
reference page:
[Mixed Model Structures](../../vignettes/22_mixed_models_vignette/mixed_model_structures.qmd).

::: callout-important
**⚠️ The confusion to avoid**

`(1|patch)` and `(1|treat:patch)` are **both random-intercept** models.
The `1` is the intercept; what differs is only the **grouping**.
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-tip
**🖐 Do I need `a/b` here?**

Only if the inner IDs **restart** inside each outer level (patch 1,2,3,4
in *every* treatment). Then R cannot tell nesting from crossing and you
must write `(1|treat/patch)`.

Our patches are numbered 1–16 across the whole study, so `(1|patch)`
already says it.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ "boundary (singular) fit"**

A variance was estimated as **exactly 0** — the likelihood hit the edge
of what a variance is allowed to be. It is the REML version of the
moment estimator going negative (Part 4).

Simplify the random effects; do not ignore it.
:::
::::
:::::::

## Wrap-up

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
Today you:

- Decided **fixed vs random** by asking whether you care about *these*
  levels or about *how much they vary*
- Learned a random factor costs **one parameter** where a fixed one
  costs *k* − 1
- Read `(1|group)` correctly, and saw it is **not** a random slope
- Chose between the ***F*-test (*p* = 0.091)** and the **Wald χ²
  (*p* = 0.043)** — and learned why the *F*-test is right at 16 groups
- Saw **where the variance components come from**: a search over a
  restricted likelihood, not a partition of sums of squares
- Got **ICC = 0.50**, and saw **partial pooling** shrink each patch
  estimate toward its treatment mean
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-important
**✅ The one idea to keep**

A mixed model does not "remove" the patch effect — it **estimates** it,
and tests the treatment against the right amount of noise.

The old way *partitioned* variation that was already computed. The new
way *proposes* variances and keeps the ones that make the data most
likely. On a balanced design they agree exactly; everywhere else only
the second still works.
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 Up next**

`glmer()` — a non-normal response **and** a random effect. You now have
both halves.
:::
::::
:::::::

## Before Next Class

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
Take the pine needle data, **collapsed to one value per team per side**
(the two-stage summary from Week 3):

``` r
p_df <- pine_df |>
  group_by(team, side) |>
  summarise(needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm),
            .groups = "drop")

anova(lmer(needle_length_mm ~ side + (1|team), data = p_df))
```

Compare *F* to the **square of** the paired-*t* statistic from Week 4
(*t* = −2.72). You should get ***F* = 7.41, df 1 and 3, *p* = 0.072** —
the paired *t*-test **is** this mixed model.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-tip
**🚀 If you finish early**

Run the same formula on the **raw 64 needles**. You get *p* = 0.057 on
**59** denominator df, not 3 — because `(1|team)` alone assumes `side`
behaves identically in every team, so all 64 needles count as
replicates of the side effect.

Now let each team have its own side difference, by adding
**`+ (1|team:side)`**. R warns **"boundary (singular) fit"**:
σ²~team:side~ comes back as exactly **0**, the df stay at 59, and
nothing is fixed. Four teams cannot separate that variance from zero —
which is why the collapsed 8-value analysis is the defensible one.
:::
:::

## Readings

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Gotelli & Ellison**, Ch. 10 — The Analysis of Variance, for the random-effects and variance-component material this lecture rebuilds.
- Hurlbert, S. H. (1984). Pseudoreplication and the design of ecological field experiments. *Ecological Monographs, 54*(2), 187–211. The Part 1 reference, and still worth reading in full.
- **Quinn & Keough** (2002), *Experimental Design and Data Analysis for Biologists*, Ch. 9 §9.1 — nested designs and expected mean squares. This is the source of today's worked example.
- Zuur, A. F., Ieno, E. N., Walker, N. J., Saveliev, A. A., & Smith, G. M. (2009). *Mixed Effects Models and Extensions in Ecology with R*. Springer. Ch. 5 is the standard ecological treatment of REML.
- Bates, D., Mächler, M., Bolker, B., & Walker, S. (2015). Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4. *Journal of Statistical Software*, 67(1), 1–48.
::::

::: callout-note
**📖 On the dataset**

The sea urchin grazing data are Andrew & Underwood's, as analysed in
Quinn & Keough Ch. 9. The textbook PDFs are on Canvas.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Why no Whitlock & Schluter**

W&S does not cover mixed models or random effects. For this topic,
Gotelli, Quinn & Keough, and Zuur are the references.
